newsitem.title: USA: S.F. Fed's Parry says pickup in inflation a risk.
newsitem.headline: S.F. Fed's Parry says pickup in inflation a risk.

text.p: U.S. inflation has been surprisingly well behaved despite tightness in labor markets but an acceleration of prices remains a risk, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco said Tuesday.
San Francisco Fed President Robert Parry said several factors, like worker insecurity and a decline in the growth of benefit costs, appear to have helped to contain labor costs.
However, in prepared remarks to the Financial Women's Association and the Financial Institutions Marketing Association, Parry cautioned that the effects of such factors were probably temporary.
"That means, if labor markets remain as tight as they are now, we risk a modest pickup in inflation in the future," he said.
"The Fed takes this risk quite seriously. Given the uncertainty about inflation, we'll have to be especially vigilant to watch for signs of inflationary pressures as the year unfolds," Parry added.

He stressed that the Fed would not want to sacrifice any of the gains it has made so far in the fight against inflation and that it hopes to continue to make progress toward the ultimate goal of price stability.
Regarding the outlook for inflation in 1997, the San Francisco Fed chief said the surprisingly good performance last year made it hard to predict what lies ahead.
"Given the high levels of resource utilization -- especially the tight labor markets -- I would have expected inflation to pick up a bit in 1996," Parry said.
"Instead, the (Consumer Price Index) excluding food and energy grew at only a 2.6 percent rate through November 1996 -- down about half a percentage point from 1995," he said.

Looking at overall economic growth, Parry said data on the fourth quarter of 1996 have shown "considerable strength," suggesting that the rather moderate 2.1 percent rate of growth in the third quarter "may have been just a 'pause.'"

"This suggests that 1997 is starting off with considerable momentum," Parry said, adding that he would not be surprised if the economy grew at least as fast as the long-run trend rate of around two percent.

"That means we're not likely to see civilian unemployment go much above its current rate of 5-1/4 percent, nor is it likely that capacity utilization rates in manufacturing will drop much below their recent levels of almost 83 percent," Parry said.
